entries.note: Literally breaking the night's fast; it once meant any meal after going without food, as used by [[see:William Shakespeare]] and [[see:John Dryden]].
A meal hobbits must have, and one of the many meals that once made up an English day.
Probably a shortening of [[from:luncheon]], which is cited first; supposedly means a lump, as [[see:hunch]] relates to [[see:hump]] and [[see:bunch]] to [[see:bump]].
A small snack eaten around 11 in the morning, between [[see:breakfast]] and [[see:lunch]].
What posh people call their evening meal; when Rob was growing up it was a small meal after [[see:dinner]], just before bed.
One of the many separate meals once eaten in an English day, especially on country estates.
An old meal eaten around six o'clock, which explains why some people call their evening meal [[see:tea]].
An old snack in the English day; France still has one as [[see:quatre-heures]], a sweet snack around four in the afternoon.
A little sweet snack the French eat around four in the afternoon, the counterpart of [[see:fourses]].
Etymologically the first meal of the day, sharing a Latin root with [[same-root:déjeuner]] and [[same-root:desayuno]]; it moved to midday, then to evening around the Industrial Revolution.
What Rob's part of England calls the last meal of the day, a name linked to the old meal of [[see:high tea]].
Rob's French word for breakfast, meaning to break one's fast: a negative prefix plus [[from:jeûner]], to fast; same Latin root as [[same-root:dîner]].
Spanish for breakfast, meaning to break one's fast, with the negative des-; like [[same-root:déjeuner]], it shares a Latin root with [[same-root:dinner]].
The French name for their last meal of the day, from the same Latin root as [[same-root:déjeuner]], so the French break their fast twice.
A Germanic animal name; once on the Norman ruling class's plate, the meat got the French-derived name [[see:pork]].
A Germanic animal name; once on the Norman ruling class's plate, the meat got the French-derived name [[see:beef]].
A Germanic animal name; once on the Norman ruling class's plate, the meat got the French-derived name [[see:poultry]].
A French-derived word for meat on the Norman plate, in contrast to the Germanic [[see:pig]]; a classic example of Anglo-Saxon and Norman class dynamics.
A French-derived word for meat on the Norman ruling class's plate, in contrast to the Germanic [[see:cow]].
A French-derived word for meat on the Norman ruling class's plate, in contrast to the Germanic [[see:chicken]].
A Germanic food word that once meant a crumb or morsel as well as bread; its root means to bubble or boil, from rising [[see:yeast]].
In Old English any food, nourishment or meal, from a root meaning moist or wet; by the 1300s it meant flesh, replacing [[see:flesh meat]].
Food is to [[same-root:feed]] what [[see:blood]] is to [[see:bleed]]; it meant fuel and nourishment, and is related to [[same-root:fodder]] and [[same-root:foster]].
The meaning of the root of [[see:meat]]; the word is a well-known [[see:word aversion]], reportedly disliked by about 20% of people.
A strong dislike of a particular word, such as [[see:moist]], which reportedly about 20% of people share.
What meat in today's sense was called when [[see:meat]] meant any food, much like the German and Dutch words for meat meaning flesh.
An old word for a butcher, discussed on an earlier episode, in line with [[see:flesh meat]].
An old term for vegetables from when [[see:meat]] meant any food; Jess says it feels almost like a [[see:kenning]].
An old term for dairy products from when [[see:meat]] meant any food.
A metaphorical compound used in Old English poetry such as Beowulf, like [[see:whale road]] for the sea.
An Old English [[see:kenning]] for the sea.
An Old English [[see:kenning]] for the brain.
Means to froth or bubble, like the root of [[see:bread]].
An animal's pancreas used as food; the bread part may come not from [[unrelated?:bread]] but from a similar Old English word meaning flesh.
From the Latin word for bread, like [[same-root:companion]]: someone you share bread with.
From the Latin word for bread, literally someone you share bread with, like [[same-root:company]].
Contains the same Latin root for bread as [[same-root:companion]].
Contains the same Latin root for bread as [[same-root:companion]].
Contains the same Latin root for bread as [[same-root:companion]].
From Old English [[from:hlāfweard]], loaf-ward: someone who looked after your bread, another word for someone you eat bread with.
Literally a bread maid or bread maker, someone who kneads bread; from the same root as [[same-root:knead]].
Knead with a K, meaning to massage dough rather than to need; from the same root as [[same-root:lady]].
Ground grain such as flour, from a root meaning grind and directly related to [[same-root:mill]]; unrelated to meal meaning a repast, despite the matching spelling.
A repast, from a Germanic root meaning time, as in German [[same-root:Mal]], which makes mealtime tautologous; unrelated to meal meaning flour.
Directly related to [[same-root:meal]] in the sense of flour, which a mill or miller would make.
German for time, as in [[see:einmal]], [[see:zweimal]] and [[see:nochmal]]; it shares the Germanic root that gave English [[same-root:meal]], the repast.
German for once, literally one time, built on [[see:Mal]].
German for twice, literally two times, built on [[see:Mal]].
German for again, literally another time, built on [[see:Mal]].
Long assumed to extend [[see:lunch]], like [[see:puncheon]] and [[see:truncheon]], but cited first; it appeared around the 1600s, probably modelled on [[from?:nuncheon]].
Paired with [[see:puncheon]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
Paired with [[see:punch]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
Paired with [[see:truncheon]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
Paired with [[see:trunch]] as a model for how [[see:luncheon]] was assumed to extend [[see:lunch]].
A Middle English word for a noon draught or noon drink of ale, older than [[gave?:luncheon]], which was probably modelled on it.
Hunch is to [[see:hump]] as [[see:lunch]] is to lump.
Paired with [[see:hunch]] to show how [[see:lunch]] relates to lump.
Bunch is to [[see:bump]] as [[see:lunch]] is to lump.
Paired with [[see:bunch]] to show how [[see:lunch]] relates to lump.
Paired with [[see:truth]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:true]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:growth]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:grow]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:dearth]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Paired with [[see:dear]] as a correlation like the one between [[see:lunch]] and lump.
Blood is to [[see:bleed]] what [[see:food]] is to feed.
Paired with [[see:blood]] to show how [[see:food]] relates to feed.
Brood is to [[see:breed]] what [[see:food]] is to feed.
Paired with [[see:brood]] to show how [[see:food]] relates to feed.
Obviously related to [[same-root:food]].
Originally meant to feed; it can be read as [[same-root:food]] plus an old suffix -ster.
An old word for food itself, readable as foodstuff, related to [[same-root:food]].
An old term for food taken on a journey; Jess first heard it as whey food and thought of curds and cheese.
A bottle of beer you take along on your way to drink more beer somewhere else, a German counterpart to [[see:way food]].
Has no scientific definition; originally an adjective meaning capable of life or growing, from Latin [[from:vegetare]], to animate, so technically humans are vegetables too.
Botanically a berry; from the Aztec language, where it means the swelling fruit, and introduced to Europe only after the age of conquest.
Botanically not a berry, unlike [[see:tomato]], because its seeds are on the outside.
A Southern US salad of coconut flakes, marshmallows and canned fruit, named after [[from:ambrosia]], the food of the gods.
The food of the gods, literally meaning immortal or that which does not die; the source of the name [[gave:ambrosia salad]].
The French for meat, from the Latin for a living thing, which Rob links to the meaning of [[see:ambrosia]].
A guessing-game formula naming three categories of things, reflecting the original sense of [[see:vegetable]] as anything capable of life.
Has the same -able ending as [[see:vegetable]].
Has the same -able ending as [[see:vegetable]].
Once simply the word for any fruit, as discussed on an earlier episode, so it turns up in the origins of many fruit names.
The original name for the [[see:date]].
Originally called a [[see:finger apple]]; the word comes from Greek [[from:daktylos]], also meaning finger.
Cucumbers were once called [[see:earth apple]]s.
An old name for the [[see:cucumber]], and the meaning of the Greek word behind [[see:chamomile]].
From a Greek word meaning [[see:earth apple]], or apple on the ground; uses the same word for apple as [[same-root:melon]].
Draws on the same Greek word for apple as [[same-root:chamomile]].
Adapted via French from Latin [[from:malum persicum]], Persian apple.
Literally an apple with many seeds, from Latin [[from:pomum granatum]]; related to [[same-root:grenade]].
Related to [[same-root:pomegranate]].
Means fruit from [[from:Tangier]]; the hosts think they touched on it in their episode on colours.
The same word as Spanish for lawyer; a folk etymology from Aztec [[from:āhuacatl]], testicle, either a mishearing or a snarky comparison of lawyers to testicles.
The Aztec word meaning testicle and also the fruit, which gave [[gave:avocado]] and, through a word for avocado sauce, [[gave:guacamole]].
From the Greek for testicle, which links it to the Aztec source of [[see:avocado]].
From Aztec [[from:āhuacamōlli]], avocado soup or sauce, built on the same word as [[same-root:avocado]], though the two share almost no letters.
A folk-etymology name for the [[see:avocado]], prompted by the sound of the original word and its green, scaly, alligator-like skin.
Another name for the [[see:avocado]], from its buttery inside.
In Middle English a word for a pine cone; the growing fruit looked like a pine cone to Europeans. Most Indo-European languages use [[see:ananas]] instead.
The word most Indo-European languages use for [[see:pineapple]], which English does not; unrelated to [[unrelated:banana]].
From an African language, probably Wolof of Senegal and Gambia; its exact meaning is unknown but thought to be finger or fingertip.
Means little [[from:vagina]], in its sense of a pod, via Spanish [[from:vainilla]], little pod.
A borrowed Latin euphemism, originally a word for any pod or sheath, now a technical term; the source of [[gave:vanilla]].
Literally precooked: developing before one's time, like something cooked a little too soon.
Since the 14th century, originally any kind of stew, sometimes made with goose, spices and wine; variants include hotchpot and hodgepot.
Borrowed from French in the 1600s, literally rotten pot, for long-stewed food; now any medley; possibly a misunderstanding of Spanish [[from?:olla podrida]].
The Spanish national soup, so called because it cooks for a long time; [[gave?:potpourri]] may be a misunderstanding of it.
A confused jumble, from French for a hash of odds and ends, combining French words meaning to make merry and to eat a lot.
Swedish for sandwich, which made Rob realise that [[gave:smörgåsbord]] means sandwich board.
Literally a sandwich board, from [[from:smörgås]], sandwich.
Named after [[from:John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich]], said to have demanded meat between slices of toasted bread during a 24-hour gambling session.
Something of a bounder whose gambling story is disputed by relatives; it was said no man held so many offices and accomplished so little.
The original [[see:sandwich]] used toasted bread, so Rob argues toasted sandwiches are the real sandwiches.
From the same Aztec language as [[see:tomato]], and originally a drink.
From the Haitian word [[from:batata]], originally meaning [[see:sweet potato]]; brought to Europe after the age of imperialism began.
The original potato, though not closely related to the white potato; for centuries called [[see:common potato]]es because it was more popular.
An old name for the [[see:sweet potato]] when it was more popular than the white potato.
An old name, like [[see:Virginia potato]], for white potatoes grown in North America and considered lower quality.
An old name, like [[see:bastard potato]], for white potatoes grown in North America.
A bulbous growth on a plant below ground; Rob had to look it up.
Means salted in Greek and Latin; it once meant any dough, pastry, paste or porridge, implying a salted or seasoned mass of food.
From the same salt-related root as [[same-root:pasta]].
From Latin [[from:sal]], salt.
From the same Latin root for salt as [[same-root:salami]].
From the same Latin root for salt as [[same-root:salami]].
From the same salt root as [[same-root:salami]]; originally brined vegetables, later extended to any mixture of vegetables.
The hosts think it also comes from the same salt root as [[same-root?:salami]].
Supposedly from Roman soldiers being paid in salt, a story both hosts suspect may not be true.
From a Germanic root meaning back, perhaps buttocks, the same root as back; it once vaguely meant pork before narrowing to bacon.
The meatier, less fatty bacon preferred in Britain; tautologous, since [[see:bacon]] itself comes from a word meaning back.
An American cut that is actually the shoulder, perhaps because it is a large heavy lump, like a [[from?:butt]], or cask.
Apparently means trouser leg, perhaps because a folded calzone resembles folded trousers, though this is debated.
Supposedly from the Greek for chamber pot; Romans used it for a cooking pot, and the dish was named after the pot it was cooked in.
A dish named after the vessel it is cooked in, like [[see:lasagna]].
A dish named after the vessel it is cooked in, like [[see:lasagna]].
Named after the French cooking dish it is made in, like [[see:lasagna]].
Origin a bit of a mystery: from a word for rifle wadding, perhaps because it is light and filling; in Spanish it meant any light lunch.
